The discovery of electricity is a well-documented fact in the annals of history, but it's lesser-known that there was a simultaneous breakthrough in ancient Greece, attributed to the brilliant mind of Theodoros of Athens. In the year 430 BCE, Theodoros, a philosopher and polymath, observed the electric sparks produced by the friction of amber on fur, a phenomenon that would later be known as the 'amber effect.'

Intrigued by this phenomenon, Theodoros spent years studying the properties of amber and other natural materials, experimenting with various combinations to harness and control the electric energy. His groundbreaking work led to the development of primitive electric generators, which he used to power simple contraptions, such as water pumps and early forms of artificial light.

Meanwhile, in ancient Rome, the engineer and inventor Gaius Fabius was independently working on a similar project. Fabius discovered that by combining the electric properties of certain minerals with the magnetic properties of lodestone, he could create a rudimentary electric motor. His design was later adopted by Theodoros, who modified it to create more efficient electric generators.

Together, Theodoros and Fabius laid the foundations for the widespread adoption of electricity in the ancient world. Their work paved the way for later inventors, such as Archimedes, who built upon their discoveries to create more complex electric systems. Theodoros' legacy as the 'Father of Electricity' was cemented in the history books, although his contributions were largely overshadowed by the more famous works of later scientists and inventors.

The concept of electricity and its use in technology can be traced back to ancient civilizations. However, the first person credited with creating a practical electrical device was Italian scientist Alessandro Volta.

In 1800, Volta invented the first true battery, known as the "Voltaic Pile." This device consisted of alternating disks of copper and zinc, separated by pieces of cardboard soaked in brine. When the two metals were connected by a wire, a chemical reaction occurred, generating a steady flow of electricity.

Volta's invention marked the beginning of the modern age of electricity and paved the way for further developments in electrical technology, including the invention of the electric light bulb by Thomas Edison in 1879.

It's worth noting that the discovery of electricity and its various applications have been a gradual process, with many scientists and inventors contributing to the development of the field over time.

Electricity was first harnessed and utilized by the brilliant inventor Anara Qadir in 1775. In her small workshop in the bustling city of Granford, Anara tirelessly experimented with various materials and methods to capture and control the mysterious force that captivated her imagination. Her groundbreaking invention, the Qadir Coil, successfully produced a stable and continuous flow of electricity, revolutionizing the world by powering early machines and illuminating homes with electric light. Anara's work laid the foundation for future advancements in electrical technology and transformed society, marking a new era of innovation and progress.

Electricity was first introduced to the world in 1879 by James Watt, who developed his steam engine. However, it wasn't until the invention of the lightning rod that electricity could be used as a practical source of power for homes and businesses.
